title: SoK: Privacy-Preserving Data Synthesis
abstract: As the prevalence of data analysis grows, safeguarding data privacy has become a paramount concern. Consequently, there has been an upsurge in the development of mechanisms aimed at privacy-preserving data analyses. However, these approaches are task-specific; designing algorithms for new tasks is a cumbersome process. As an alternative, one can create synthetic data that is (ideally) devoid of private information. This paper focuses on privacy-preserving data synthesis (PPDS) by providing a comprehensive overview, analysis, and discussion of the field. Specifically, we put forth a master recipe that unifies two prominent strands of research in PPDS: statistical methods and deep learning (DL)-based methods. Under the master recipe, we further dissect the statistical methods into choices of modeling and representation, and investigate the DLbased methods by different generative modeling principles. To consolidate our findings, we provide comprehensive reference tables, distill key takeaways, and identify open problems in the existing literature. In doing so, we aim to answer the following questions: What are the design principles behind different PPDS methods? How can we categorize these methods, and what are the advantages and disadvantages associated with each category? Can we provide guidelines for method selection in different realworld scenarios? We proceed to benchmark several prominent DL-based methods on the task of private image synthesis and conclude that DP-MERF is an all-purpose approach. Finally, upon systematizing the work over the past decade, we identify future directions and call for actions from researchers. 4696 2024 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

Consequently, there has been an upsurge in the development of mechanisms aimed at privacy-preserving data analyses. Introduction Recent years have witnessed an array of groundbreaking scientific achievements across various sectors, including but not limited to medical analyses [ 1, 2], home automation and robots [ 3, 4], face recognition [ 5, 6], and malware detection systems [7, 8]. These significant strides in practical applications can be attributed to the evolution of hardware technology, refinement of algorithms, and most importantly- the availability of large-scale datasets for learning tasks or analytic workflows. While data serves as the critical fuel, the analysis of such large-scale datasets can often lead to privacy breaches. Examples range from exposing a driver's working hours and location through the data collected for training autonomous 1. ∗ indicates equal contribution. Correspondence to: Yuzheng Hu <yh46@illinois.edu> and Fan Wu <fanw6@illinois.edu>. vehicles [9, 10], to the reconstruction of data used in training machine learning classifiers [ 11, 12], and even the potential exposure of personal identities from medical images or records [13, 14]. The consequences are severe: the average cost of a healthcare data breach was of $ 9.2M [15]. In response to the escalating pace of data collection and analysis as well as the underlying privacy risks, regulatory bodies worldwide have enacted numerous legislations. No- tably, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996 introduced the privacy rules for disclosing medical records [ 16], and the Federal Rules of Civil Proce- dure guide the disclosure of court records [ 17]. These legisla- tions have exerted considerable impact on various industries. For instance, non-compliance with HIPAA has resulted in substantial financial penalties, with fines reaching as high as $1.25M [18] and $ 6.9M [19]. Amidst the convergence of regulations, penalties, cybersecurity threats, and heightened user awareness [ 20], the academic community has embarked on various research endeavors aimed at facilitating data analysis in a privacy-preserving manner. These investigations encompass a range of paradigms, such as interactive and non- interactive query processing [ 21, 22], data mining [ 23-25], machine learning [26-30], among others. However, creating privacy-preserving solutions tailored to each specific data analysis task is a formidable challenge that necessitates extensive customization. An alternative involves synthesizing a dataset devoid of private information that can be used for any downstream task, enabling “ exploratory, open-ended, and iterative ” [ 31] analyses. In contrast to the aforementioned paradigms, synthetic data permits the execution of a variety of downstream tasks without requiring modifications to the original algorithms to meet privacy constraints. This offers flexibility in terms of future task options, whilst mitigating concerns over privacy leakage. In this paper, we focus on such privacy-preserving data synthesis (PPDS) approaches. It's important to note that the uninformed application of privacy mechanisms to the original data could result in significant utility loss [ 32]. To this end, PPDS mechanisms require delicate design choices to maintain the privacy-utility trade-off. Motivation. Research of PPDS in the past decade has demonstrated a shift of focus compared to earlier works due to the following emerging challenges: • High-Dimensional and Unstructured Data. Classical PPDS approaches designed for tabular data [ 33, 34] en- counter obstacles in coping with the rising dimensionality 4696 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00002 of data and the inherent complexity involved in handling unstructured data such as images and text. • Advanced Attacks. Traditional anonymization-based PPDS approaches which adopt either the syntactic pri- vacy [35] or less rigorous privacy principles are known to suffer from various privacy attacks [36-40]. To alleviate concerns associated with the data-related challenges, statistical models ( e.g., hidden Markov model (HMM) [ 41] and Bayesian network [ 42]) and tools ( e.g., copula [ 43]) have been used to facilitate the modeling and deconstruction of high-dimensional structured data, while deep generative models [ 44-46] arise as powerful tools to handle unstructured data. To remediate concerns on the privacy front, research is focused on developing rigorous privacy notions (e.g., differential privacy (DP) [ 47]) with corresponding privacy mechanisms, as well as their adaptations and applications in different scenarios. With abundant work exploring the intersection of these two lines of research at hand, we believe it is time for us to take a step back and systematically review the established toolkits and the lessons learned. Standing Point and Contributions. Our work joins a small family of surveys (see “Related Work” below) that study PPDS. While we are not the first to review this topic, we position our work as the first to systematize the research effort over the past decade which tackles the emerging challenges using the most up-to-date toolkits . Specifically, we make the following contributions: • We present a comprehensive overview of PPDS (Section 2), considering different privacy notions and mechanisms, input data types as well as utility evaluation protocols. • We distinguish two primary research directions in PPDS: statistical methods and deep learning (DL)-based methods. Furthermore, we present a master recipe (Fig. 1) that unifies these approaches, encompassing the algorithms falling within each category. • Under the master recipe, we dissect the statistical methods (Section 3) into choices of modeling and representation, and investigate the DL-based methods (Section 4) by different generative modeling principles. To consolidate our findings, we provide comprehensive reference tables, distill key takeaways, and identify open problems in the existing literature. • We benchmark the DL-based methods for private image synthesis (Section 5), and identify DP-MERF [ 48] as the best practice. We further note that the pessimistic conclusion on synthetic tabular data by Stadler et al. [49] does not fully extend to the image domain. • We delineate future directions for researchers (Section 6). Related Work. Prior surveys related to PPDS can be classified into two categories: (i) privacy-preserving data pub- lishing (PPDP) [40, 50-53] which focuses on the anonymiza- tion of structured data, and (ii) privacy-preserving deep generative models [54, 55]. Apart from these works, we also identify a few benchmarks [ 56, 57] for some representative algorithms on private tabular data synthesis, as well as a general introduction to synthetic data [58]. Scope. In terms of the timeline, we collect papers after 2010 which allows us to concentrate on DP, and also distance ourselves from a prior survey [53]. Our ontology is as follows: Section 3 primarily concerns the intersection of database and privacy, whereas Section 4 concerns the intersection of DL and privacy. In terms of thetarget, we exclude works that only facilitate learning tasks or analytic workflows [ 59-62], or those that publish aggregated or summary statistics [ 63, 64] rather than generating synthetic data. 2. Preliminaries Given an input dataset D, we aim to design a PPDS algorithm P , such that P (D) → D′ with D′ being the synthesized dataset which is both private and utilitarian. For- mally, P satisfies a specific privacy definition (Section 2.1); and D′ attains high utility (Section 2.2). 2.1. Privacy Notions and Mechanisms There are numerous definitions of privacy spanning dif- ferent applications and time-periods [ 65-68]. In the context of PPDS, we adopt the perspective of F. T. Wu [ 67], which posits that privacy remains intact if no violation, in the form of re-identification, occurs. We deal with a broad sense of re- identification beyond human identities [ 69-72] and consider the exposure of any sensitive information within data as re- identification. This could range from unveiling connections among users in social networks [ 73], to revealing sensitive facial attributes, such as the eyes, nose, or mouth, in facial image data [74]. We focus on differential privacy (DP), which pro- vides mathematical guarantees against re-identification. Pri- vacy definitions such as syntactic anonymity [ 35] (e.g., k- anonymity [75] and its variants) and less rigorous privacy principles such as obfuscation [ 76] were widely adopted in PPDS [40, 53]. However, recently, there is a clear tendency to prefer DP [ 77-79] because of (i) its ability to quantify privacy leakage, and (ii) the stronger protection it offers [ 80]. Differential Privacy (DP). Along with a variety of benign properties including composability [ 81], immune to post- processing [82] and future-proof [ 83], DP has become the gold standard of privacy. DP quantifies and limits the amount of knowledge one could learn by observing the algorithm's output. Formally: Definition 1 ((ε, δ)-DP [ 82]). Let X be the space of the dataset, a randomized algorithm M with domain N|X | is (ε, δ)-differentially private iff for all S ⊆ Range(M) and for any neighboring datasets D and D′ differing by one record: Pr[M(D) ∈ S ] ≤ eε Pr[M(D′) ∈ S ] + δ. The standard definition assumes a centralized database with trusted server and independence between partici- pants [ 35]. R ´enyi DP (RDP) [ 84] is a variant of DP that uses R ´enyi divergence [85] to measure the distance between two probability distributions. Other variants include edge-DP and node-DP [86] for graphs (see Section 3.3). Privacy Mechanisms. For algorithms with numeric output, DP and its variants are typically enforced by adding noise (Laplace and Gaussian mechanism [ 82]). For non-numeric 24697
